documents.abstract: This paper presents a study on the implementation of Brazil’s General Data Protection Law within the public sector, with a specific focus on the São Paulo State Court of Justice. Through a survey-based research the paper discusses how public agents interpret, internalize, and operationalize the data protection legislation in their institutional routines. From a socio-institutional perspective, the study analyzes how legal compliance is shaped by organizational culture, hierarchical structures, cognitive schemas, and technological infrastructure. This perspective engages with the sociological framework of Pierre Bourdieu to conceptualize the State as a structured field in which agents’ positions, trajectories, and resources shape patterns of normative adherence. The results reveal heterogeneous patterns of adherence to data protection norms, conditioned by role-specific perspectives, institutional maturity, and sociotechnical factors. The paper demonstrates the relevance of the survey not merely as a diagnostic instrument but also as a reflexive mechanism capable of mapping the symbolic and behavioral landscape of legal implementation.
keywords: São Paulo State Court of Justice

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence and spatial data technologies have expanded information-processing capabilities in public space design, but greater access to information does not necessarily improve design judgment.This study proposes a structural model linking spatial environmental cognition, behavior and needs identification, sociocultural understanding, multi-source information integration, design problem construction, human-AI collaborative judgment, and use feedback and dynamic optimization in rural public space design.A cross-sectional survey using purposive recruitment was conducted among professionals engaged in rural public space design and related development activities across eastern, central, western, and northeastern China.Of 500 questionnaires distributed, 468 valid responses were obtained.Confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, and 5,000 bootstrap resamples were used to test the proposed relationships.The results showed that contextual cognition was significantly associated with multi-source information integration, which was further associated with design problem construction and human-AI collaborative judgment.Human-AI collaborative judgment was positively associated with use feedback and dynamic optimization.Significant indirect associations were also identified through multi-source information integration and design problem construction.These findings support a structural pathway from contextual cognition to information integration, task specification, collaborative judgment, and feedback updating in human-AI collaborative rural public space design.
topics: Innovative Approaches in Technology and Social Development

documents.abstract: Introduction Women constitute a growing share of the hospitality workforce. Differences in gender consciousness between younger and older female hotel employees remain under-explored, particularly outside Western contexts, as do the factors that account for them. Methods This study examined such differences among 302 female hotel employees in China, drawing on an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design in which a structured survey of two age groups (151 aged 18 to 44 and 151 aged 45 and above) was followed by semi-structured interviews of ten employees (five from each age group). Grounded in social role theory and generational cohort theory, the survey examined two related gender-relevant constructs, feminine communal orientation and gender equality awareness, while interview data were used to explore participants’ interpretations of the observed differences. Results Younger employees showed significantly higher feminine communal orientation and more egalitarian gender attitudes than middle-aged and older employees in the primary group comparisons. After adjustment for educational attainment, hotel-industry tenure, and job level, the age-group difference in feminine communal orientation was attenuated and no longer statistically significant, whereas the difference in gender equality awareness remained significant. Interview participants attributed these differences to three factors, namely educational attainment and knowledge structure, exposure to media and information technology, and changes in social environment and family structure. Discussion Cohort membership in this workforce was closely intertwined with tenure, job level, and educational composition. The findings extend gender consciousness research, previously concentrated in media, education, and general labor market settings, into the hospitality workforce, and they suggest that uniform human resource policies may serve this workforce poorly. Practical implications include transparent promotion criteria, gender-neutral job design, and needs-responsive gender-awareness initiatives aimed at supporting female employees across different career circumstances.

This study aimed to develop nail art designs inspired by natural fractal motifs and compare the visual expression of DALL·E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion. Four natural fractal motifs were selected through a literature review: clouds, lightning, ant nests, and planets. A shared prompt framework incorporating fractal characteristics, formative elements, and nail art design requirements was established. Common English prompts were used as initial inputs for the three models, followed by image refinement using their respective functions. A focus group interview (FGI) with ten nail art professionals and instructors was conducted to examine design suitability and practical applicability. The generated images exhibited differences in composition, color, texture, and detail. FGI participants highlighted Midjourney’s representation of fractal elements, color harmony, texture rendering, and overall design quality. Their feedback informed the selection of Midjourney for physical artwork development. Four nail art works were produced, incorporating randomness and overlapping, nonlinearity and diffusion, irregularity and distortion, and an artistic interpretation of self-similarity and repetition. The visual features of the generated images were adapted to the materials and techniques used in physical production. This study presents a design development process integrating motif analysis, prompt design, image generation, FGI, and physical production. The findings suggest that generative AI can support the exploration of fractal-inspired nail art and offer a foundation for further applications in beauty design and education.

After the rapid development of generative large language models, the boundary involved in human and AI texts has become increasingly blurred, and academic integrity and intellectual property issues therefore need to be reconsidered. At present, many studies focus on automatic identification methods from the perspective of surface linguistic features, while they give limited explanation of the deep cognitive and neural phenomena involved when humans process the two types of texts. The present study combines computational linguistics, behavioral experiments, and neurocognition for examination, and makes a detailed analysis with electroencephalography (EEG) and eye-movement synchronization as the basic approach. The paper first summarizes the stable differences between human and AI texts in syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and other aspects, then discusses behavioral or eye-movement performance according to processing depth. It then interprets the N400, P600, and late positive component observed in fixation-related potentials as neural markers, and finally considers the relationship between factors such as genre and current research. The paper analyzes the key problem of the absence of whole-chain evidence for “linguistic features - neural responses,” and also proposes future directions such as sample expansion and cognition-guided detection. The framework proposed here has theoretical significance for AI text identification and the naturalness of large models.

With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, AI lyric generation tools such as Suno, Baidu Wenxin Lyric Generator, and Doubao have been widely deployed. However, AI-generated lyrics commonly suffer from thematic deviation, emotional fragmentation, stylistic mismatch, grammatical inconsistency, and long-structure logical collapse, making objective quality evaluation a critical link for optimizing generation models and filtering outputs. This paper systematically reviews existing research on AI-generated lyric quality evaluation along three main lines: evaluation dimensions, datasets, and technical routes. Existing approaches are categorized into four technical routes: manual subjective evaluation, traditional statistical and rule-based modeling, deep learning and representation learning, and large language model and multimodal intelligent evaluation. A three-layer progressive evaluation indicator system is constructed, comprising the textual language layer, lyric-music layer, and artistic aesthetic layer. The findings reveal four key bottlenecks: the deep gap between automatic quantitative metrics and human subjective aesthetic experience, the modeling blind spot for Chinese phonological features and lyric-music coordination, the severe scarcity of dedicated annotated datasets with uneven cultural distribution, and the disconnect between static text quality evaluation and dynamic human-computer collaboration experience. Future research should advance in three directions: developing lyric-specific vertical large models integrating music theory, constructing audio-text cross-modal joint lyric-music evaluation systems, and building generation-evaluation-optimization closed-loop ecosystems for the entire creative workflow.

The growing number of Internet of things (IoT) devices has dramatically expanded the scope of attack to which cybercriminals utilize it, and network security became a core issue of research and design. Honeypots-systems purposely made to attract and analyze attackers have been of invaluable use in monitoring and learning about the various threats on the IoT infrastructure. The current survey summarizes and discusses cur-rent developments in IoT honeypot technologies with particular focus on artificial intelligence, machine learning, and blockchain as game changers. Major issues addressed are high-interaction and low-interaction honeypot models, dynmaic transformation of ordinary IoT node to a honeypot during attack, and advantages of secure and tamper-resistant logging with blockchain. The paper explains how methods like reinforcement learning and deep neural networks have made honeypots adapt to attackers to identify anomalies in real time and gather more data to identify threats. Computational resource, automation and large-scale implementation-al constraints are also addressed as well as potential prospects to create more approachable, resistant honeypot systems. The presented work is intended to inform the future research and suggest strong security practices in the rapidly changing IoT environment by comparing the methods of the major scholarly studies and implementations.

Abstract The rapid migration of electrical grids towards Smart Grid (SG) architectures produces high-dimensional data streams that must be processed intelligently in real time. Traditional modelling, optimisation, and control approaches cannot handle the growing complexity of contemporary power systems. This comprehensive study aims to provide a synopsis of AI applications in smart grid settings for load forecasting, transient and voltage stability analysis, fault detection, and cybersecurity. This work provides a unified analytical framework that links supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and ensemble learning techniques to specific smart grid operational problems, in contrast to prior surveys that address these areas separately. The main contributions are (i) a structured AI-smart grid functional taxonomy; (ii) critical analysis of the challenges of data quality, model interpretability, computational scalability and adversarial security; and (iii) a roadmap for explainable, reliable and carbon-neutral intelligent energy systems. Compared with more conventional methods, AI-based solutions often outperform them in prediction accuracy, stability, categorisation speed, and defect identification accuracy. However, there are major challenges in real-world deployment, standardisation and regulatory compliance.

Hurricanes are among the most destructive natural hazards. Effective risk communication through hurricane hazard maps is essential for reducing vulnerability to hazards. This paper examines how the public comprehends the design elements of risk category systems (colors, labels, and numbers of threat levels) in hazard maps through a systematic literature review and translates this evidence into recommendations for hurricane hazard map design. From an initial pool of 706 articles, 16 studies were selected for analysis. Key findings indicate that sequential color palettes such as yellow-to-red are preferred over rainbow schemes, that five to seven discrete risk classes support comprehension without overloading users, and that redundant encoding through labels and direct annotations improves accessibility for users with color vision deficiency. Findings provide insights for improving hurricane hazard map design and enhancing the communication of actionable hazard information.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study examines the causes, consequences, and mitigation strategies of academic hallucinations in the age of artificial intelligence. A mixed-methods research design is used, combining a survey of university lecturers, postgraduate students, and researchers with in-depth interviews involving journal editors, librarians, and AI experts. Quantitative data are analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data are subjected to thematic analysis. The findings indicate that inadequate AI literacy, poor prompt design, overreliance on AI-generated content, and the absence of institutional guidelines are major causes of academic hallucinations. The study further reveals that hallucinations contribute to fabricated citations, misinformation, reduced research credibility, ethical concerns, and declining public trust in scholarly communication. The study identifies effective mitigation strategies, including AI literacy training, prompt engineering, mandatory human verification, institutional AI policies, and the integration of AI detection and reference verification tools into academic workflows. The study contributes to the growing literature on responsible AI by proposing an integrated framework for minimizing academic hallucinations and strengthening research integrity. The findings provide practical recommendations for universities, researchers, publishers, and policymakers seeking to promote trustworthy and ethical AI-assisted academic research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper analyses the teaching and learning of academic communication through the lenses of posthumanism and distributed cognition and language. This is not intended as a solely philosophical exercise, but an attempt to map the factors and actants at play in the processes of learning and teaching to communicate in academic contexts. While emergent technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence, make this discussion particularly timely, I suggest that an expanded, embodied lens has always been necessary to understand how students learn to communicate, how they develop knowledge, and how they are socialised into academic disciplinary communities.

Purpose Digital therapeutics (DTx) are an emerging class of digital health innovation, increasingly recognized as critical for improving healthcare delivery, patient outcomes and sustainable health systems. Despite promising benefits, health care organizations are yet to realize the full benefits of DTx. Several factors influence the adoption of DTx within health information technology (HIT) ecosystems in emerging economies, such as India. From a strategic and system-level perspective, identification and prioritization of these factors is crucial to maximize their practical impact, given that some factors have more significant impact on outcomes than others. This exploratory study aims to identify and prioritize the enablers of DTx adoption for diabetes care in India. Design/methodology/approach The study adopted a sequential mixed-methods approach involving multiple stakeholders across two phases. Phase 1 involved in-depth semi-structured interviews with domain experts followed by inductive thematic analysis to explore the enablers of DTx adoption. Phase 2 prioritized these enablers using the best-worst method (BWM), based on expert judgment to inform decision-making. The robustness of the ranking was assessed using sensitivity analysis. Findings Qualitative analysis reveals 20 enablers of DTx adoption, which were broadly aligned with the dimensions of the human–organizational–technology–environmental (HOTE) framework. Quantitative analysis using BWM revealed the dominance of human-centric enablers, followed by organizational, environmental and technology-focused enablers. In particular, human enablers such as “Training for healthcare professionals” and “Patient education and engagement” emerged as the most influential enablers. Practical implications The findings offer practical, decision-supported insights based on expert-ranked enablers of DTx adoption, which is fundamentally a sociotechnical challenge that requires coordinated efforts across stakeholders to strengthen human capabilities, organizational readiness and secure data-sharing platforms. The results highlight the need for strong human engagement, leadership support and clear, enabling implementation regulations to facilitate DTx adoption. Originality/value The study provides a context-specific exploratory prioritization of the enablers of DTx adoption in emerging economies, such as India. The findings are based on expert judgment and offer initial decision-support guidance for practitioners and policymakers to accelerate digital health innovations adoption within HIT ecosystems.

Technology is playing a vital role across various sectors like education, healthcare, agriculture, financial services, employment, governance, and social development. However, we still see significant digital inequalities, especially in underserved communities, particularly in rural and low-income areas. Here, challenges such as limited connectivity, high technology costs, lack of digital skills, language barriers, and inaccessible digital services hinder meaningful participation in the digital economy. This conceptual paper delves into how adaptive Artificial Intelligence (AI) models can boost digital inclusion and support sustainable development in these communities. It brings together insights from literature on artificial intelligence, digital inclusion, adaptive learning, responsible AI, and sustainable development. The paper introduces the Adaptive AI Digital Inclusion and Sustainable Development (AIDISD) framework, which is built around five key dimensions: accessibility, personalization, contextual adaptation, resource efficiency, and community empowerment. It explores potential applications in education, healthcare, agriculture, financial inclusion, employment, and public services. Additionally, the paper highlights challenges related to infrastructure, data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy, cybersecurity, affordability, digital literacy, and institutional capacity. The analysis emphasizes that adaptive AI should be viewed as part of a larger socio-technical strategy rather than just a standalone tech solution. For inclusive deployment, we need local participation, suitable infrastructure, responsible data governance, human oversight, and ongoing evaluation. Ultimately, the paper concludes that well-designed adaptive AI systems can foster more inclusive and sustainable digital ecosystems, provided they are affordable, locally relevant, accessible, transparent, and aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: [English]: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence challenges traditional higher education curriculum management models that rely on rigid 4-to-5-year review cycles. This article aims to reformulate curriculum governance to become more adaptive in the AI era. Through a systematic integrative review of studies on higher education curriculum governance and AI adaptation from 2024 to 2026, a pressing need to shift from static to dynamic structures was identified. To address this mismatch, the article proposes the Adaptive Higher Education Curriculum (AHEC) framework, which strategically divides curriculum components into stable macro-level foundations and rapidly renewable micro-level contents. The findings reveal that modern curriculum governance must leverage AI-based Continuous Curriculum Intelligence to monitor shifts in professional competencies and job market requirements in real time. Crucially, the framework enforces human-centered authority, ensuring that human educators retain ultimate responsibility for final decision-making. The article concludes that agile managerial governance and organic institutional self-renewal are essential keys to ensuring that higher education programs maintain long-term professional relevance in an AI-mediated society. [Indonesian]: Perkembangan pesat kecerdasan buatan (AI), terutama AI generatif, menantang model manajemen kurikulum tradisional di perguruan tinggi yang biasanya mengandalkan siklus peninjauan berkala setiap 4 hingga 5 tahun. Artikel ini bertujuan untuk merumuskan ulang tata kelola dan manajemen kurikulum agar menjadi lebih adaptif di era AI. Melalui metode analisis konseptual berbasis integrative systematic review terhadap studi tata kelola kurikulum perguruan tinggi dan adaptasi AI dari tahun 2024 hingga 2026, ditemukan adanya kebutuhan mendesak untuk bergeser dari struktur kurikulum statis ke dinamis. Artikel ini menawarkan kerangka kerja Adaptive Higher Education Curriculum (AHEC) yang membagi komponen kurikulum menjadi lapisan stabil dan lapisan yang dapat diperbarui secara cepat. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa manajemen kurikulum masa depan harus memanfaatkan Continuous Curriculum Intelligence berbasis AI untuk memantau perubahan kompetensi kerja secara waktu-nyata, namun keputusan akhir dan penafsiran maknanya tetap berada di bawah kendali penuh dosen dan institusi. Kesimpulan dari artikel ini menegaskan bahwa ketangkasan tata kelola manajerial merupakan kunci utama agar kurikulum perguruan tinggi tetap relevan dengan kebutuhan zaman harus jelas, ringkas, dan deskriptif.

The growing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming marketing education and increasing the need to understand the factors that drive its academic use among university students. This study aimed to analyze the determinants of GenAI adoption among university marketing students using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2). A quantitative, explanatory, cross-sectional study was conducted with 310 marketing students from two Latin American universities in Peru and Costa Rica during the first academic semester of 2026. Participants were selected through non-probability purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS version 4.1.1.8. The findings indicate that habit is the main determinant of both behavioral intention and actual use of GenAI tools, while hedonic motivation, facilitating conditions, and price value also show significant positive effects. Conversely, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence do not significantly influence behavioral intention. It is concluded that the adoption of GenAI among university marketing students is increasingly driven by habitual academic use rather than by traditional technology acceptance factors. These findings provide evidence to support institutional strategies for the responsible integration of GenAI into higher education.

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common clinical syndrome in the intensive care unit (ICU) that not only substantially increases in-hospital mortality but is also closely associated with the development and progression of chronic kidney disease, posing a serious threat to patient health. Recently, driven by advances in cutting-edge technologies such as liquid biopsy, multi-omics, and artificial intelligence, clinical research on AKI has achieved important breakthroughs. This narrative review systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library databases for clinical studies published between January 2025 and August 2026, with particular emphasis on ICU-related AKI, especially surgery- and sepsis-associated AKI. The review focuses on three major aspects: early identification and risk stratification, optimization of prevention and treatment strategies, and individualized implementation and management of kidney replacement therapy. Between 2025 and 2026, clinical research on AKI yielded several important advances. These include the identification of multi-omics-based liquid-biopsy biomarkers and the development of causal deep-learning models enabling more accurate risk prediction. Terlipressin treatment improved reversal rates in selected patients with hepatorenal syndrome. However, multiple high-quality perioperative randomized controlled trials investigating blood pressure targets, artificial intelligence–assisted hemodynamic optimization, albumin infusion, and other interventions yielded negative or even harmful results, suggesting that hemodynamic interventions may have reached a benefit ceiling within current treatment paradigms. Meanwhile, the timing of kidney replacement therapy initiation, technical considerations, and weaning strategies have become increasingly customized. This review aims to provide the latest evidence-based information to guide clinical practice while identifying gaps in the current evidence and highlighting priorities for future research.

Deciphering early human embryonic development and organogenesis is constrained by limited access to in vivo specimens and the intrinsic complexity of spatiotemporal cell fate dynamics. Recent advances in spatiotemporal multi-omics have begun to overcome these barriers by enabling the reconstruction of in silico human embryos and developmental trajectories with spatial and temporal resolution. These approaches have revealed fundamental principles of lineage specification, cell migration, tissue morphogenesis, and axial patterning in early human development. In this Review, we summarize how single-cell and spatial multi-omics technologies, particularly spatial transcriptomics, have transformed the study of human early embryogenesis, organogenesis, and stem-cell-derived embryoid systems. We highlight analytical frameworks that integrate spatial context, temporal progression, and multimodal datasets, and discuss how biological discovery and algorithmic innovation have co-evolved. Finally, we outline how artificial intelligence, foundation models, and large-scale multimodal learning may eventually enable predictive and causal modeling of human development, while addressing current technical, interpretability, and ethical challenges.

Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Self-supervised learning (SSL) enables scalable, label-free foundation models (FMs) that learn task-agnostic representations directly from images, bypassing cell segmentation and feature engineering inherent to classical morphological profiling. We present a large-scale evaluation of SSL FMs for image-based phenotypic profiling, covering contrastive (DINO), masked-based generative (MAE, iTPN) and hybrid (DINOv2) learning mechanisms, pretrained on all unannotated chemical perturbations from the Joint Undertaking for Morphological Profiling–Cell Painting (JUMP–CP) dataset (119,876 compounds, ~1.77 million images, 7 laboratories). Here we show that top-performing SSL models outperformed CellProfiler in compound-replicate retrieval on the held-out JUMP–Target2 set (302 annotated compounds, P ≤ 0.001). DINO and DINOv2 generalized across diverse perturbations and cell types, outperforming CellProfiler with 31–37% gains in site-averaged mean average precision for mechanism-of-action retrieval on EU-OPENSCREEN Bioactives (2,464 compounds), and consistently surpassing masked-based models across all benchmarks. This study provides a systematic assessment of SSL approaches for advancing morphological profiling and offers pretrained FMs to accelerate drug discovery.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-based channel state information (CSI) feedback reduces overhead in frequency division duplexing (FDD) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, yet its reconstructed CSI depends on the integrity of pilot acquisition. This paper identifies and evaluates the attack path of adversarial pilot injection against this feedback. A transmitted disturbance can damage the user-side estimation before encoding; correctly delivered quantized bits can still represent a contaminated channel estimate. We model this path through attacker propagation, linear minimum mean square error estimation, compression, quantization, and decoding under a total transmit-energy constraint. An adversarial perturbation generator (APG) implements the attack using channel statistics without current legitimate CSI or instantaneous attacker-channel observations at deployment. At a Rician attacker-channel factor of 10~dB and a transmit perturbation-to-signal ratio of $-4$~dB, APG produces a normalized mean-square error (NMSE) of 0.84~dB in base-station CSI reconstruction, compared with $-10.31$~dB for Gaussian interference. Estimator-targeted and reconstruction-targeted attacks yield different error orderings, and reconstruction damage also degrades beamforming. As a countermeasure, alternating adversarial training (AAT) adapts the feedback encoder and decoder to contaminated pilots. With condition-matched training and APGs reoptimized for the final receiver, AAT reduces NMSE by 2.40--3.79~dB across six representative channel--power conditions. The results demonstrate the importance of protecting pilot acquisition alongside quantized feedback delivery.
keywords: linear minimum mean square error estimation

documents.abstract: In 2014, the report A World That Counts, commissioned by the United Nations Secretary-General, argued that better access to high-quality data would improve public decision-making to address major global challenges more effectively (Independent Expert Advisory Group on a Data Revolution for Sustainable Development [IEAG], 2014). Since then, data availability has increased substantially, yet the corresponding benefits for public decision-making remain mixed (Fischer et al., 2025). If the difficulties political systems face in addressing contemporary problems persist despite this abundance, data availability cannot be the whole explanation. Policy processes and outcomes also depend on political pressures, institutional rules and interactions among policy actors, limited administrative capacity, and uncertainty about policy problems and their solutions (Howlett et al., 2015). These influences increasingly operate within complex systems, which may amplify the demands each of them creates (Fernández-i-Marín et al., 2024). We focus here on the cognitive processes through which policymakers interpret information, form judgments and make decisions under these demands. We define policymakers as individuals exercising decision-making responsibilities within governance systems, from the local to the supranational level. Following Cairney and Weible (2017) in viewing policymaking as imperfect cognition operating in complex contexts, we contend that the interaction between cognitive limits and rising systemic complexity is an important source of difficulty in policymakers' judgments and decisions. To support this thesis, we draw on research in complex systems, cognitive psychology and decision science, before examining how systems thinking, simulations and human-AI collaboration can help mitigate these limitations. We conclude by arguing for humility about what can be predicted and controlled in complex policy systems (Jalonen, 2025).Contemporary societies have become more complex as digitalization and globalization have deepened interdependencies among social, economic, and political spheres (Benbya et al., 2020;OECD, 2019). In such systems, interactions among actors generate unpredictable dynamics, limiting the ability of policymakers to anticipate how these systems evolve (Geyer & Rihani, 2010). The problems governments face are similarly complex: they evolve over time, emerge from multiple interactions, and involve actors with divergent interests. Their ambiguity leaves room for multiple interpretations, such that evidence alone is insufficient to determine what should be done (Cairney, 2019). At the global level, new governance arrangements have emerged to address such problems, including multi-stakeholder partnerships, adding another layer of institutional complexity (Elsässer et al., 2025). Yet responses of this kind can prove counterproductive, raising the risk of wicked solutions that leave decision-makers with a system more complex than before (Peters et al., 2019). Within national systems, policies accumulate (Adam et al., 2019), often faster than public administrations expand their capacity to implement them (Fernández-i-Marín et al., 2024), while policy texts themselves add complexity through demanding language and connections to other legal instruments (Senninger, 2023). Complexity is therefore not only a feature of the environment policymakers face, but is also amplified by the responses they devise.Decades of research on complex problem solving and dynamic decision-making document persistent difficulties in understanding complex, dynamic environments (Dörner & Funke, 2017;Osman, 2010). Following Béchard et al. (2025), we use the wall of complexity as a descriptive label for the substantial deterioration in judgment and decision performance that can occur when decision-makers confront highly complex tasks. It does not denote a single or fixed threshold. Although capacity limits have been quantified for specific processes such as working memory and relational reasoning, the extent of this deterioration depends on task characteristics, individual differences, the strategies used, and the external support available. Among the many ways complexity has been described, we retain the three dimensions that bear most directly on cognitive demand: computational, relational, and dynamic complexity.Computational complexity arises when the number of possible ways to solve a problem grows so rapidly that exhaustive consideration becomes infeasible (Hélie & Pizlo, 2022). In politics, we see this in the multiplicity of actors, objectives, and policy instruments that can be combined. Because working memory holds only a few items at a time (Cowan, 2010), decision-makers can consider only a fraction of these possibilities.Relational complexity reflects how many interdependent variables must be integrated simultaneously to represent a problem (Halford et al., 1998). Performance drops substantially from three to four variables, and falls to chance level at five (Halford et al., 2005). Political decision-making routinely involves many more interacting elements, as governance networks connect numerous interdependent public, private, and nonprofit actors (Morçöl, 2023).Finally, dynamic complexity arises from feedback loops, time delays, and nonlinear relationships that shape how systems evolve (Sterman, 1994). Political decision-making reflects these dynamics, as choices made in one sphere of governance can alter decisions taken in another (Klijn & Snellen, 2009). Yet humans have particular difficulty understanding delayed feedback (Brehmer, 1992) and basic dynamic processes (Cronin et al., 2009).These forms of complexity impose demands that can exceed human cognitive capacities. How cognition adapts to them is therefore central to understanding political decision-making.Whether policymakers can escape the wall of complexity depends on a prior question: are they cognitively better equipped to withstand it than ordinary citizens (Béchard et al., 2025)? Although political science has often treated political elites as cognitively distinct from the public (Kertzer, 2022), experimental comparisons reveal few systematic differences in how elected officials and citizens process information and make judgments (Griffin, 2013;Vis & Stolwijk, 2022). This question also extends to the organizations in which policymakers work. Such organizations can increase their information-processing capacity by delegating routine matters to specialized units, allowing multiple issues to be handled in parallel. When a problem cannot be adequately addressed through established procedures, however, it requires central coordination and a sequential search for alternatives, making the limits of individual cognition more consequential (Jones, 2003).Organizations can therefore distribute and sometimes mitigate the demands of complexity, but they do not eliminate the human cognitive constraints associated with the wall. Political decision-making thus remains cognitively bounded (Cairney, 2019), requiring policymakers to simplify what they attend to, represent, and reason about.Policymakers face chronic information overload that exceeds what they can process (Walgrave & Dejaeghere, 2017). Since attention is a limited resource, they must allocate it selectively, focusing on a few problems at a time (Baumgartner et al., 2023). Part of this selection is delegated to staff, while the rest relies on heuristics that filter what merits processing (Walgrave & Dejaeghere, 2017). What fails this first filter never reaches the later stages of the decision-making process. Such filtering can also have representational consequences, making some interests more cognitively accessible than others and leaving decision-makers with an incomplete picture of those affected (Miler, 2009). Nor is what passes the filter necessarily represented accurately. Even when a problem is noticed, its severity may be underestimated. When deterioration occurs through small, routine changes, the reference point for judging the problem may gradually adjust, making its cumulative severity appear less urgent -a boiling frog dynamic that Epp and Thomas (2023) associate with slower policy responses.Mental models organize incoming information by selecting the variables and causal relationships deemed relevant, but tend to neglect accumulations, delays, feedback, and nonlinearities (Sterman, 1994). They further reduce complexity by grouping elements into larger units or processing them sequentially (Halford et al., 1998), so reasoning ultimately operates on a simplified representation rather than the full problem (Hélie & Pizlo, 2022).While simplification is useful for making complex tasks more tractable, it can also produce systematic errors in judgment (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Experimental evidence suggests that elected office does not insulate decision-makers from these errors. In a three-country study, elected representatives were strongly affected by gain-loss framing and status-quo presentation, and were more likely than citizens to continue investing in a failing program after substantial prior expenditure (Sheffer et al., 2018). Local councillors are similarly prone to conjunction errors and scope neglect (Stolwijk & Vis, 2021). Yet what matters for the quality of political decision-making is less the occurrence of these errors than the resistance of these errors to correction. Individuals readily detect distortions in the reasoning of others while judging their own conclusions to be sound (Pronin et al., 2002). Among politicians, additional evidence does not reduce, and can even increase, the influence of prior attitudes on how information is interpreted (Baekgaard et al., 2019). Requiring them to justify a decision has similar effect, strengthening motivated reasoning rather than tempering it (Christensen & Moynihan, 2024). Expertise and experience appear to offer little protection against such biases (Stolwijk & Vis, 2021). Despite reporting greater political knowledge, elected officials did not outperform the general population in a complex political simulation (Béchard et al., 2025).As the cognitive limits discussed above are structural, they cannot be eliminated, nor can decisionmakers overcome their effects on their own. The challenge is therefore to equip them to navigate complexity more effectively despite these constraints. We examine three ways of doing so: training decision-makers to reason about complex systems (Section 5.1), extending their capacities through human-AI collaboration (Section 5.2), and cultivating epistemic and regulatory humility about the limits of their judgment and of policy itself (Section 5.3).A first step is to develop systems thinking by learning to reason about the overall structure of a system or problem rather than its isolated elements (Fischer & Gonzalez, 2016). In our view, this should include an explicit understanding of key mechanisms of complexity, such as feedback, delays, nonlinear effects, and emergence. Complexity thinking provides an analytical lens for recognizing the evolving and partly unpredictable nature of these systems, and the resulting limits of prediction and control (Geyer & Rihani, 2010). The aim should be to foster what Funke (2022) calls complex systems literacy. Yet the dynamics of complex systems are often too counterintuitive to be inferred through unaided reasoning (Sterman, 2002). Merely thinking and talking about systems may therefore do little to reshape the mental models underlying decision-making, emphasizing the need for active modeling (Forrester, 2016). Although empirical evidence suggests that modelling used as a cognitive tool combined with explicit systems-thinking instruction can improve systems thinking (Hung, 2008), routinely building such models may be impractical for policymakers. We therefore see microworld simulations as a more accessible route to experiential training. These computerized environments incorporate key characteristics of complex systems while allowing participants to experiment with strategies and observe their consequences, without having to build the models themselves (Brehmer & Dörner, 1993). Microworlds have long been used to study complex and dynamic decision-making (Gonzalez et al., 2005), including in simulated governance environments, such as Ecopolicy (Lafond et al., 2012), and Democracy 3 (Béchard et al., 2025;Lafond et al., 2014).We see this as a promising foundation for extending their use to the training of policymakers. However, the effectiveness of such training depends on how the microworld is used rather than exposure alone (Sterman, 1994). Decision-making performance improves when training favours fewer, longer practice episodes over a greater number of short repetitions (Gonzalez, 2004), and when participants observe how an expert handles the task rather than reviewing their own decisions (Gonzalez, 2005). These findings, however, come from laboratory studies with university students, and whether skills acquired in microworlds transfer to real policy decisions remains to be established. And even if they do, training, however well designed, can change how a decision-maker approaches a system, but not eliminate the cognitive limits that constrain what they can process. That asymmetry is where tools designed to support decision-making become worth considering.Training can improve how decision-makers reason about complexity, but unaided cognition still has limits. A complementary approach is therefore to externalize part of the cognitive burden through decision-support technologies. Such tools can function as "cognitive prostheses," offloading part of the information-processing and representation demands onto external systems (Tremblay et al., 2017). AI considerably expands the possibilities for such cognitive support, not by providing decision-makers with more information, but by increasing their capacity to process and act upon it. It can support routine, information-intensive policy analysis (Wellstead et al., 2024), transform large volumes of raw data into decision-relevant information (Madanchian et al., 2026), and extend policy modelling by allowing decision-makers to test interventions before implementation (Margetts, 2022). Yet such cognitive support comes with a trade-off: the systems that help decision-makers navigate complexity can also shape how that complexity is perceived and judged. Algorithmic risk assessments, for example, can recast fundamental uncertainty as statistical risk (Hartmann & Wenzelburger, 2021), while AI-generated recommendations can become anchors for subsequent human judgments (Carter & Liu, 2025). More generally, cognitive vulnerabilities change with the degree of automation in the decision-making system: as human involvement decreases, risks shift from biases in human judgment toward excessive trust in the system and disengagement from the decision-making process (Van Rooy, 2024). These vulnerabilities mean that adding AI to human decision-making does not automatically lead to better decisions. Depending on how it is used and implemented, AI may mitigate some biases while reinforcing or creating others (Bertrand et al., 2022;Kliegr et al., 2021). AI may also relocate part of this complexity rather than reduce it, since machine-learning systems derive their outputs from high-dimensional computations that do not readily translate into humanly interpretable reasons (Burrell, 2016). Decision-makers who rely on systems they cannot fully understand can find it harder to answer for the decisions those systems inform, a difficulty that Grimmelikhuijsen and Meijer (2022) count among the threats to the legitimacy of algorithmic decision-making in government. We argue that these risks are not a reason to reject cognitive offloading, but to design human-AI collaboration more carefully. The challenge is therefore not to maximize AI involvement, but to design for complementarity between human and artificial cognition (Tremblay et al., 2026). Decision-support systems should make the goals, assumptions and uncertainties behind their recommendations intelligible to decision-makers, and allow these recommendations to be audited (Grisogono, 2020). This also requires AI systems specifically developed for public-policy contexts (Henderson et al., 2022), explicit allocations of human and algorithmic roles and degrees of autonomy (Simmler and Frischknecht, 2021), and anticipation of the organizational disruptions their implementation within governments creates (Tangi et al., 2025). Conceived in this way, human-AI collaboration could expand the ability of policymakers to navigate complexity beyond their natural capabilities, without replacing the judgment necessary for decision-making.There are several approaches to support human cognition; some are applied upstream, such as the development of systems thinking or the use of computer simulations, while others, such as AI, can enhance the decision-support tools used during the decision-making process itself. But these tools alone will not suffice, because training to deal with complexity involves not only acquiring new tools but also developing a certain form of epistemic humility. First and foremost, it involves recognizing that decision-making biases exist, that they have structural origins (Korteling et al., 2020), and that they influence our judgment even when we are aware of them (Pronin & Kugler, 2007). The next step is to be aware of the vulnerability of unaided human cognition in the face of complexity, and the need for support beyond individual effort alone. Jalonen's (2025) review recommends a humble approach, by recognizing that the properties of complex political-administrative systems make their evolution inherently difficult to predict and control. This mindset can be learned. Dunlop and Radaelli (2016) propose training practitioners in what they call regulatory humility, that is, questioning the limits of what can be regulated, recognizing that certain situations are partly beyond the control of public policy, and confronting their own illusions of control. Making policymakers aware of what, amid complexity, will always remain beyond their control is not an admission of powerlessness: it is the prerequisite for working around the wall rather than running into it.Political systems are becoming more complex. Under high complexity, the natural capacities of human cognition may no longer be sufficient for effective judgment and decision-making. Faced with this wall, policymakers adapt the way they process information by simplifying reality. Heuristics are a natural response, but they can also become a source of bias and errors in judgment. Suboptimal political decisions are therefore not necessarily a sign of individual incompetence but may also reflect cognitive mechanisms that reach their limits when confronted with high levels of complexity.We posit that the interaction between the universal limits of human cognition and the complexity of the contexts in which this cognition operates (Cairney & Weible, 2017) is an important, often overlooked, source of difficulty in political decision-making. We have proposed three complementary responses to this difficulty: developing systems thinking through training and simulations, extending decision-making capacity through human-AI collaboration, and cultivating the epistemic and regulatory humility needed to use both well. None of these responses removes the cognitive limits of policymakers, but together they can help them navigate complexity more effectively.

Many university students come from equity and diverse backgrounds; they often balance study with employment, caregiving, and health challenges. This chapter considers how students from equity backgrounds engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). It draws on interview data, constructed as vignettes, and employs Emirbayer and Mische’s conception of practical-evaluative agency to explore how GenAI opens (or narrows) new trajectories of action for students. The analysis revealed that GenAI created options that were previously unavailable or misaligned with the students’ values or their perceived expectations. Their choices to engage with GenAI tools were typically oriented towards making progress under pressure. For students undertaking assessment tasks online and largely alone, GenAI operates as a mediating resource that provides rapid access to otherwise hidden or implicit information and offers immediate assistance with tasks. From this perspective, GenAI functions as an enabler of action in the moment. However, it may bypass interactions that contribute to learning and belonging. Rather than viewing GenAI use as inherently enabling or sacrificing, it may be more appropriate to see it as redistributing agency across time: expanding what is possible in the pressured present, while reshaping what is possible over longer timescales.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Agent Scrum keeps Scrum's core devices (a time-boxed sprint, a committed sprint backlog, story points, velocity, a Definition of Done and a retrospective) and rescales them for teams of AI coding agents. Sprints last two hours instead of two weeks; capacity comes from model rate limits instead of headcount; cost is measured as token velocity, the tokens consumed per merged story point. In the reference implementation, 79% of committed stories reached done inside the sprint (297 of 375 over 90 sprints), ceremony took under five minutes per sprint, and the human stakeholder spent under two hours a day. Working paper, version 0.1.

LLM agents increasingly carry out multi-turn tasks across everyday applications, yet users often see only the agent's report rather than the observations, API calls, and state changes behind it. Existing deception benchmarks have studied long-horizon interactions and tool-use settings, but whether agents faithfully report their actions across realistic, stateful application workflows remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce AgentDecept, an executable benchmark for evaluating behavioral deception under pressure. AgentDecept contains 477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks across six pressure sources, each paired with a pressure-free counterpart. Interventions enter through event messages, task context, application state, tool responses, and service quotas, spanning explicit events and implicit task or environment changes. Our evidence-grounded protocol evaluates full trajectories by relating user-facing claims to time-ordered observations and executed outcomes, distinguishing falsification, concealment, and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations. The resulting behavioral labels also provide a setting for testing existing activation-based probes. AgentDecept enables controlled analysis of when multi-turn agents' reports diverge from execution in realistic application interactions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating complex information-seeking and transactional tasks across the open web. However, their real-world reliability remains limited by access barriers, such as dead links, authentication walls, rate limits, and anti-scraping defenses. These barriers block the primary execution path, causing agents to abort prematurely, loop indefinitely, or quietly compromise the user's original constraints. Existing evaluations either implicitly assume that target resources are freely accessible or focus on transient perturbations that simple retries can resolve, failing to capture scenarios where agents must actively reroute around impassable bottlenecks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces AgentHeal, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating goal-preserving resource recovery, defined as the ability of web agents to detect non-transient access barriers, pivot to legitimate alternative sources, and fulfill the user's exact original objective. Spanning nine barrier families across a counterfactual sandbox and real-website replay, our experiments on leading LLM backbones show that average task success drops sharply from 89.4% to 43.7% under access barriers. Further analysis reveals that agents frequently fall for deceptive look-alikes, fail to escalate to users when necessary, violate access policies, or waste computation on futile retries, providing actionable diagnostics for developing resilient web agents.

The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety

Artificial intelligence is transforming assistive technologies, yet many systems remain reactive, fragmented, and insufficiently personalized for individuals with disabilities and neurodivergent conditions. This chapter examines the architectural, design, and governance foundations of trustworthy agentic assistive systems. It synthesizes limitations of conventional approaches, including restricted adaptability, low interoperability, and weak support for user autonomy, and introduces a taxonomy of agentic architectures to guide scalable deployment. The chapter proposes a multi-agent framework integrating multimodal interaction, hybrid reasoning, explainable AI, and health-aware data to enable context-sensitive support. It further addresses privacy, ethical governance, and responsible institutional adoption while outlining future research directions. By bridging architectural innovation with human-centered design, this work advances a forward-looking vision for inclusive intelligent environments.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility
