Using a conceptual narrative review of foundational authentic-leadership scholarship, occupational health frameworks, and research on leadership and employee well-being, the article develops an integrative explanation rather than reporting new empirical data. The analysis suggests that authentic leadership may support mental health when leaders communicate honestly, respond consistently, invite employee voice, and make decisions transparently. These behaviors can reduce interpersonal uncertainty and help employees access social and psychological resources. However, authenticity should not be equated with unrestricted self-disclosure, moral infallibility, or the replacement of professional mental-health support. Its benefits depend on organizational conditions, leader competence, workload, fairness, and access to adequate resources. The article proposes practical implications for leadership development, job design, and employee well-being evaluation, and identifies testable propositions for future empirical research.

Learner autonomy has become an essential objective of English language teaching, particularly in higher education, where students are expected to assume increasing responsibility for their own learning. Furthermore, digital technologies and artificial intelligence have transformed autonomous language learning by providing personalised support. The present study investigates autonomous language learning practices and perceptions among undergraduate engineering students studying English as a Second Language (ESL). The research aimed to evaluate the extent to which students demonstrate autonomous learning behaviours and self-regulated learning skills, identify the resources they use, examine perceived benefits and challenges, and explore their intentions to continue autonomous language learning after graduation. A quantitative survey was conducted among 65 bachelor’s degree engineering students enrolled in an English for Specific Purposes course at the National Technical University of Ukraine «Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute». Data were collected through an anonymous questionnaire consisting of multiple-choice and Likert-scale items and analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, median values, and interquartile ranges. The findings indicate that students actively engage in technology-supported autonomous learning, with AI tools, English-language videos, podcasts, and mobile applications representing the most frequently used resources. Respondents generally demonstrated positive selfregulation in goal setting, progress monitoring, and strategy adjustment, whereas self-evaluation and independent decision-making received less favourable ratings. Flexibility, personalised learning, responsibility, and digital literacy were identified as the principal advantages of autonomous learning, while lack of motivation, insufficient time, and difficulty maintaining regular study routines constituted the main barriers. The study demonstrates that students expressed positive intentions to continue learning English independently after graduation. The findings highlight the importance of integrating self-regulated learning strategies together with carefully guided use of digital technologies and AI tools to strengthen learner autonomy in ESP courses.

Objectives Identification of barriers to the development of a safety culture, determining their importance and detecting associations between them. Material and methods First, a critical and comparative literature analysis was used, followed by a quantitative empirical study. The quantitative analysis examined the frequency of occurrence as well as associations and connections between attributes. A survey was conducted on a sample of 105 people. Results It was found that the most common barriers to the implementation of safety culture in the literature are: (1) lack of leadership and commitment of management, (2) lack of commitment and disregard by employees and (3) lack of understanding by employees. On the other hand, practitioners indicated (1) lack of leadership and commitment of management, (2) problems with communication and (3) lack of commitment and disregard by employees as the most important barriers. Therefore, two of the three most important barriers are the same in both cases and concern people: management on the one hand, and employees on the other. Conclusions A characteristic triad of barriers to developing a safety culture has been identified. In this way, a model approach to the problem was proposed. Understanding them and striving to eliminate them will allow for a more effective shaping of this area of organizational culture.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Accurate recognition of food items and estimation of portion sizes from images is a key challenge in advancing dietary assessment and nutritional monitoring. In this study, we benchmark twenty-six configurations (seventeen model releases) of state-of-the-art open-source Vision–Language Models (VLMs), varying in size (≤15 GB) and number of parameters (<25B), on real-world food photographs collected in a university canteen, doing so to evaluate their potential for supporting automated nutrition logging and health interventions. Methods: We construct a curated benchmark dataset with human-annotated labels, including both food item names and scale-measured portion sizes, and assess model predictions based on recognition performance and mean absolute error in the portion estimate. The semantic matcher used to score food recognition is validated against a panel of human judges, and all results are reported with bootstrap confidence intervals and stochastic replicates. Results: Our experiments show that the VLM qwen2.5vl:7b achieves the highest overall performance in food identification (F1=0.68), outperforming other open-source models in terms of precision and F1 score. Under the human-validated semantic matcher, it also outperforms the more recent successors of the same model families, which nevertheless improve portion estimation and, under a threshold-free LLM judge less sensitive to verbose descriptions, match or exceed it in recognition. For comparison, we evaluate five proprietary models (four OpenAI generations and one Anthropic model) as a benchmark and find that they tend to outperform open-source VLMs in both food recognition (best F1=0.77, GPT-4o) and portion size estimation error; notably, however, the most recent proprietary generations do not improve on their predecessors for this task under our evaluation protocol. Conclusions: These findings highlight the potential and current limitations of general-purpose VLMs in fine-grained food understanding tasks, with implications for the design of scalable, vision-based dietary assessment systems in digital health.

This educational initiative explored the integration of generative AI and authentic human interaction in smoking cessation counseling training among approximately 150 pharmacy students at the Faculty of Pharmacy, Chiang Mai University, Thailand. Implemented in July 2026, the program combined repeated individual counseling practice using a generative AI tool, counseling with a real person who smoked, structured self-reflection, classroom discussions, and peer role-play. Students reported that AI offered convenient, repeatable practice in a lower-pressure environment. However, AI occasionally misunderstood spoken input or provided off-target responses. However, AI occasionally misunderstood responses or provided unrealistic interactions. In contrast, counseling with real smokers offered authentic, unpredictable experiences requiring students to adapt their communication to individual needs and situations. The initiative highlights the complementary roles of generative AI and human interaction in pharmacy education, demonstrating how technology-supported practice can be combined with authentic experiences to prepare future pharmacists for real-world smoking cessation counseling.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Management of infective endocarditis (IE) is often confounded by the presence of prosthetic valves, transcatheter prostheses, and cardiovascular implantable electronic devices, as well as by changing epidemiologic risks and antimicrobial resistance patterns. For the diagnosis of IE, blood cultures and echocardiography remain foundational, but important gaps persist, particularly in culture-negative and prosthetic/device-associated infections. Contemporary diagnostic criteria and guidelines now support a multimodality approach incorporating molecular microbiology and advanced imaging. This review summarizes emerging technologies including broad-range 16S/18S/28S rRNA polymerase chain reaction and sequencing, fluorescence in situ hybridization coupled with sequencing, targeted and shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), plasma microbial cell-free DNA, cardiac computed tomography, and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography/computed tomography. We also examine the potential role of artificial intelligence in echocardiographic interpretation and of large language models in multimodal data integration. Current evidence suggests that tissue-based molecular testing generally provides greater microbiologic yield than valve culture in culture-negative IE, while blood-based mNGS and microbial cell-free DNA may extend pathogen detection after antibiotic exposure and reduce reliance on tissue-based diagnosis. However, heterogeneity in specimen handling, sequencing pipelines, contamination control, reporting thresholds, and clinical interpretation remains a major barrier to implementation. Future progress should move beyond pathogen detection toward rapid, reproducible, clinically actionable diagnosis that integrates organism identification, anatomic localization, disseminated disease, and personalized treatment. Prospective outcome trials, standardized workflows, cost-effectiveness studies, and multidisciplinary Endocarditis Team integration can help determine whether these technologies translate into better antimicrobial stewardship, procedural decision-making, and patient outcomes.

Conversational artificial intelligence has changed the way people interact with digital systems. Users can now ask questions in everyday language, receive explanations, obtain recommendations, and complete tasks without learning complicated software interfaces. However, a conversation that sounds natural is not always accurate or dependable. An AI assistant may misunderstand a question, lose track of earlier information, produce an unsupported answer, or use an external tool in an inappropriate way. These issues have become increasingly important as conversational systems move beyond simple question answering towards more autonomous tasks.This paper examines recent developments in AI-based conversational agents through a critical review of selected research published between 2024 and 2026. The 2022 scoping review by Kusal et al. provides the foundation for understanding earlier conversational technologies, including natural-language processing, deep learning, context management, and emotion-aware dialogue. More recent studies extend this discussion to large language models, autonomous agents, retrieval-augmented generation, hallucination mitigation, and agent evaluation.The review suggests that improving the language model alone is not sufficient to address the practical challenges of conversational AI. Reliability also depends on how information is retrieved, how previous conversation details are managed, how responses are checked, and how risky actions are controlled. To address these concerns, this paper proposes a Trustworthy Context-Grounded Conversational Agent Framework. The framework combines context management, evidence-based response generation, response verification, privacy controls, restricted tool access, and human intervention when necessary. The proposed framework has not yet been experimentally evaluated; therefore, its effectiveness must be established through future implementation and comparative testing

This chapter examines the evolving relationship between artificial intelligence and sustainability in tourism within the broader context of Industry 4.0 and ongoing digital transformation processes. While AI-driven technologies are widely recognized for their capacity to enhance operational efficiency, optimize resource utilization, and support sustainable development goals, they simultaneously introduce significant conceptual, ethical, and governance-related challenges. Drawing on a socio-technical perspective, this study moves beyond purely technological or outcome-oriented approaches and explores how artificial intelligence reshapes not only the operationalization of sustainability but also its meaning, representation, and lived experience within tourism systems. The chapter introduces the concept of rehumanizing sustainability as a conceptual and practical framework for addressing these challenges. This approach emphasizes the reintegration of human values, agency, and experiential dimensions into AI-driven systems.

With the ageing population's growing demand for mobility, this study examines acceptance of automated vehicles (AVs) among the near-elderly. By integrating perceived risk, behavioural inertia, and personalised adaptation into the Unified Technology Acceptance and Use Theory (UTAUT) framework, a new model was estimated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 352 licenced drivers aged 55-64 in mainland China through a national online survey. Findings reveal that behavioural inertia is not critical, whereas perceived risk is the strongest negative driver of acceptance intention. Conversely, personalised adaptation and performance expectancy are the primary positive drivers. Mediation analysis shows that personalised adaptation significantly influences intention through effort expectancy, though not through behavioural inertia. Results suggest that AV design should minimise perceived risk and provide adaptive functions, such as frequent-route memory, driving-habit adaptation, and clearer system communication, to enhance adoption among this demographic.

This is the final paper in a tetralogy examining the effects of Large Language Models (LLMs), colloquially known as Artificial Intelligences (AIs) on modern society. Previous diagnostic research (Uscroft, 2026a, 2026b, 2026c) has demonstrated that in closed statutory environments—such as law enforcement, regulatory oversight, and judicial decision-making—the intrinsic architectural properties of LLMs, notably preference-driven sycophancy and conversational fluency, present severe vulnerabilities. When deployed by institutional authorities, these properties induce epistemic laundering, obscure evidential provenance, and generate automated confirmation bias. This paper presents the necessary counterweight to that institutional critique. Grounded in sociolinguistic theory (Bourdieu, 1991; Bernstein, 1971), we examine the sociotechnical mechanics of generative LLMs from the perspective of the individual. We establish that the very architectural features deemed hazardous to institutional rigour serve as potent mechanisms for democratic empowerment and linguistic equity. We demonstrate how LLMs function as automated register translators, enabling individuals who lack formal command of institutional sociolects (academic, legal, corporate, and political) to project an authoritative voice. Furthermore, we analyse how model sycophancy—when reframed from an individual human-in-the-loop perspective—operates not as a defect, but as a catalyst for psychological safety, non-judgemental iteration, and advocacy. Through empirical case studies spanning recruitment gatekeeping, internal workplace progression, public service operational dynamics, and political representative access, this paper codifies the fundamental sociotechnical duality of generative artificial intelligence: dangerous as an uncalibrated arbiter of institutional authority, but liberating as a personal instrument of human agency.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into Higher Education requires understanding students' perceptions and competence in interacting with these technologies. This mixed-methods study examined perceptions of GenAI and documented prompt engineering competence in academic tasks among 89 Psychology and Biomedical Engineering students. Study 1 employed a 2 × 2 quasi-experimental factorial design comparing disciplinary area and instructional approach (guided vs. autonomous), complemented by thematic analysis. Students reported favourable views of GenAI, particularly for understanding, learning, guidance, and work planning, while emphasising the need to verify AI-generated information and improve reliability and contextual accuracy. No significant multivariate effects of disciplinary area, instructional approach, or their interaction were found. However, item-level analyses identified two items with higher scores under autonomous instruction after multiple-comparison adjustment. Study 2 examined documented prompt engineering competence in 24 group reports using five rubric dimensions and the exploratory Prompt Competence Index (PCI). No differences between instructional approaches remained significant after multiple-comparison adjustment, although descriptive differences in Iteration and PCI emerged among biomedical engineering reports. Overall, findings support contextualised, iterative, and critically supervised human–AI interaction, while suggesting that instructional differences are context- and indicator-specific. Further validation of the PCI in larger, diverse, and balanced samples is required.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Frontline artificial intelligence (AI) and service robotics are fundamentally transforming hospitality service encounters from traditional human-dominated touchpoints into complex, technology-infused service ecosystems. However, hospitality managers face a strategic paradox: balancing operational efficiency against relational value co-creation. Guided by Torraco's integrative review methodology, this study systematically synthesizes 29 primary source studies published across premier service management, marketing, and hospitality journals from 2004 to 2025 to reconceptualize how human–AI frontline configurations shape customer relationships. It unifies four complementary theoretical lenses: Service-Dominant Logic, Automated Social Presence Theory, the Stereotype Content Model, and the Four Intelligences Framework. It establishes a structural taxonomy of frontline configurations: AI-Led Substitution, AI-Augmented Hybrid, and Human-Led AI-Mediated encounters, and resolves three persistent empirical paradoxes. First, service robots significantly mitigate customer discomfort during awkward, embarrassing, or evaluative encounters by eliminating metaperception processing (judgment anxiety). Second, high robotic social presence is attenuated in the direct co-presence of human staff due to relative social cognition comparison penalties. Third, AI augmentation enhances customer-perceived warmth only when organizational systems convert automated time-savings into employee discretionary decision autonomy; using efficiency gains to accelerate guest throughput quotas triggers technostress, emotional exhaustion, and surface acting. Synthesizing these cognitive, affective, and organizational mechanisms into an integrative conditional process model, the study formulates six testable theoretical propositions and delineates a multi-level boundary condition matrix spanning task intelligence tiers, customer technology readiness, employee workload density, and hotel service tiers. Methodological and theoretical future research agendas are established alongside four strategic managerial directives for frontline service ecosystem design in the machine age.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being explored in tertiary emergency departments and prehospital emergency medical services because these settings combine time-critical decisions, incomplete information, and persistent operational strain. This critical narrative review examines where current evidence is strongest, where it remains limited, and what ethical and practical conditions are required for responsible adoption. The literature suggests that the most credible near-term applications are bounded forms of decision support, particularly in triage and early risk stratification, selected time-sensitive diagnostic pathways such as stroke, operational forecasting, dispatch support, destination decisions, and supervised documentation assistance. However, the field remains constrained by retrospective study designs, heterogeneous endpoints, limited external validation, uncertain transportability, uneven subgroup performance, and a persistent gap between model performance and real-world clinical usefulness. In emergency and prehospital care, these limitations matter because bias, overreliance, and poor workflow integration can rapidly translate into patient harm or operational disruption. Current evidence supports cautious optimism rather than technological inevitability. The most defensible role for AI in acute care is not the replacement of clinicians or EMS professionals, but carefully governed augmentation of human judgment through locally validated, transparent, and continuously monitored decision-support tools.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly used in molecular and multimodal oncology to identify features that influence machine-learning predictions. A model-important feature may subsequently be described as a biomarker, mechanistic driver or therapeutic target, although these labels represent distinct scientific claims requiring different evidence. We propose the XAI Biomarker Translation Matrix, a claim-specific conceptual framework separating explanation evidence (E), biological evidence (B) and translational evidence (T). A claim gate routes XAI-prioritised candidates into three validation pathways: diagnostic, prognostic or treatment-predictive biomarkers; mechanistic therapeutic targets; and tumour-selective delivery targets. The explanation dimension is XAI-specific and addresses whether attribution is defined, stable, faithful and reproducible, whereas the biological and translational dimensions connect the attributed feature to claim-appropriate evidence. Claim-evidence concordance requires terminology to remain no stronger than the evidence demonstrated for the intended use, and falsification-first translation asks investigators to prespecify the observation most capable of challenging the proposed interpretation. Complementing established AI-reporting, biomarker-validation and target-assessment standards, the matrix adds an XAI-specific explanation-evidence layer and an explicit claim gate linking attribution to claim-specific evidence and terminology: XAI prioritises candidates; the claim determines the validation pathway.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) face employment disparities despite possessing strengths valued in the workplace. One barrier is the interview, where impressions often form from nonverbal cues that commonly differ in ASD and contribute to negative evaluations. Although artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in hiring, whether these behaviors elicit AI bias is unclear. This study examined whether large language models (LLMs) assign lower ratings to candidates displaying autistic-associated behaviors and whether a debiasing procedure reduces these effects. Three LLMs rated a candidate in mock interview clips across four conditions: control (neurotypical behavior), limited eye contact, monotone speech, and low conversational reciprocity. The LLMs rated interpersonal and cognitive attributes and overall hireability before and after exposure to pro-neurodiversity research. Ratings were lower in all non-control conditions and increased after debiasing. These findings suggest LLMs may replicate bias toward neurodivergent applicants, but this bias can be mitigated.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The thirteenth edition of the GEIA Seminar brings together 48 speakers from 31 institutions across 15 countries, spanning Europe, Asia, Oceania, North and South America. The presenters and participants come from universities, research institutes, airlines, civil aviation authorities, air traffic control organizations, and private language institutions. This geographical and intellectual diversity is one of the seminar’s greatest assets. It allows us to examine familiar challenges through different lenses, learn from different operational and educational contexts, and strengthen the international connections that are essential to the development of our field. The program reflects the breadth and dynamism of current research in Aeronautical English and related areas. Our discussions range from language as a human factor in aviation safety, pilot–controller communication, shared situational awareness, and communication breakdowns to language policy, language description, and the complexities of accent comprehensibility in international aviation. The presentations also explore language assessment and proficiency testing, including questions of validity, communicative efficiency, and the competencies required of Aviation English trainers and assessors.

Stereo foundation models provide strong cross-domain generalization but remain computationally expensive for real-time and resource-constrained deployment. We propose BRD-Stereo, a bilateral reliability distillation framework that transfers foundation-model stereo knowledge to a lightweight BANet-style student. BRD-Stereo treats reciprocal left–right correspondence after geometric warping as an exchange symmetry and uses localized symmetry violations from occlusion or mismatching to reduce teacher reliability. BRD-Stereo models the spatial reliability of teacher supervision and aligns different forms of teacher knowledge with the student’s detail/smooth aggregation structure. The detail branch receives boundary- and gradient-aware supervision, while the smooth branch is guided by low-frequency disparity consistency and local plane regularization. Reliability cues from left–right consistency, image disparity edge agreement, local regularity, occlusion-aware validity, and available teacher confidence weight the pseudo-label objectives. Sliced score distribution distillation transfers a locally softened disparity target around the teacher prediction without requiring full teacher cost volume supervision. Experiments on Scene Flow, KITTI, ETH3D, and Middlebury show consistent gains over plain pseudo-label distillation, with the largest improvements concentrated in boundary, occlusion, weak-texture, and large-disparity regions while preserving BANet-scale inference efficiency.
topics: Advanced Image and Video Retrieval Techniques

documents.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnosis may benefit from gut metabolic information associated with brain-gut interactions, yet existing models largely analyze cerebral glucose metabolism alone. Although whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) can provide paired brain-gut observations, routine brain examinations rarely include gut imaging, limiting direct use of this information for diagnosis. In this paper, we present BRIDGE (Brain and Gut Representation Integration via Distribution-Guided Enhancement), a two-stage framework for transferring brain-gut metabolic knowledge to brain-only diagnosis. Specifically, BRIDGE integrates a conditional brain-to-gut latent transport module and a disease-evidence-guided cerebral pathway to capture subject-specific cross-organ correspondence and disease-relevant cerebral representations. For the cerebral pathway, a large language model (LLM) helps organize literature-derived descriptors into human-approved semantic anchors that guide feature learning. Additionally, we introduce a counterfactual-guided residual fusion mechanism, which uses matched and non-matched virtual-gut evidence to supervise a confidence gate and dynamically regulate the contribution of transported cross-organ information. At inference, BRIDGE exploits complementary gut-related context using brain PET alone, without measured gut PET. Extensive experiments across public and private cohorts demonstrate that BRIDGE outperforms brain-only and cross-organ baselines, achieving AUC gains of 6.0% and 5.2% over its brain-only counterpart for CN/MCI and CN/AD diagnosis, respectively. Notably, its ability to transfer complementary brain-gut metabolic context while preserving brain PET as the sole inference input highlights its potential for clinically practical diagnosis. Our code is available at https://github.com/CUHK-AIM-Group/BRIDGE.

Abstract Occupational respiratory disease (ORD) surveillance remains largely reactive, with diagnosis often occurring only after clinically significant symptoms develop. Existing risk stratification tools are primarily clinically derived and rarely incorporate occupational exposure variables such as exposure intensity, duration, and workplace hazards, limiting early identification of at-risk workers. This review synthesizes current evidence on predictive modelling and risk stratification tools for respiratory diseases, evaluates their applicability to occupational health, and proposes a data-driven framework for proactive risk stratification. A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2021 and 2025. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms related to occupational respiratory diseases, predictive modelling, prognostic tools, and occupational exposure assessment were combined using Boolean operators. Extracted data included study characteristics, modelling approaches, predictors, and model performance metrics, which were narratively synthesized using thematic mapping. Of 618 records identified, six representative evidence approaches were retained for detailed comparative synthesis. Clinical models such as BODE and DOSE provided useful prognostic information but lacked occupational exposure parameters. Exposure-based approaches showed associations between cumulative exposure and respiratory outcomes, while a meta-analysis of machine-learning models for acute respiratory distress syndrome reported a pooled AUC of 0.7407. Key predictors included age, smoking status, lung function, and exposure-related factors. Current reactive and clinically focused approaches limit effective ORD prevention. Integrating occupational exposure variables into predictive, data-driven risk stratification frameworks is essential for early identification of high-risk workers. The proposed ORDiRS framework represents a step toward proactive occupational health surveillance in industrial settings.

Background: Contemporary healthcare institutions generate daily very large amounts of data, which contain highly useful information for the improvement of work organization, planning and overall efficiency. While models and techniques to extract these insights are well known and constantly developed in mathematical biology, complex systems physics and data science, the adoption of these techniques among Clinicians and Hospital Administrators remains limited, mainly due to language and methodological divides. Objective: In this article we implement an AI Multi Agent System (MAS) that allows Users to use predictive models and make statistical analyses via natural language conversations. Methods: We developed EpidemIA, a training-free MAS endowed with a modular suite of epidemiological models written by human experts, executable on a single-GPU workstation. To avoid relaying sensitive data to third parties, the system uses locally an open-weights LLM as backbone for its two subagents. Results: Using a dataset of Emergency Department visits provided to us by IRCCS Sant'Orsola (Bologna) we test the model on a few typical use cases, demonstrating the possibility of performing both simpler statistical analyses and visualizations as well as more complicated epidemiological predictions based on dynamical models, through simple queries made in natural language. Conclusions: While still being a proof-of-concept implementation, EpidemIA showcases the transformative capabilities of LLM based technologies as an enabling factor in the widespread adoption of complex dynamical models, which is at present hindered by their steep learning curve.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In the medical field, artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms have driven significant advancements, particularly in cancer detection and treatment. AI’s ability to mimic human cognition, such as intelligent behavior and critical reasoning, is invaluable for analyzing complex medical data. AI has the potential to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, and patient outcomes of cancer detection, given the disease’s pervasive global impact. AI in imaging diagnostics reduces radiologists’ workload and increases cancer screening sensitivity, contributing to decreased incidence of this deadly disease. This chapter outlines biomedical image processing fundamentals, including pre-processing, feature extraction, and segmentation. It then explores various AI-based techniques in cancer diagnosis, such as image analysis, CAD, pathology analysis, genetic analysis, and risk assessment. This chapter discusses AI algorithms like convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, recurrent neural networks, GANs, support vector machines, and neural networks in cancer detection. Real-world case studies demonstrate AI’s effective use in breast cancer detection via 60 mammography, CT-based lung cancer screening, pathology-based diagnosis, and genomics-based personalized treatment. This chapter addresses challenges and future directions, including ethical and regulatory concerns and AI integration with metaverse and exascale computation to enhance cancer detection.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in the public sector presents opportunities to transform administrative processes and services, but it demands institutional capacities that ensure responsible, transparent, and sustainable use. This study aimed to analyze the institutional readiness of the Ecuadorian public sector for the responsible adoption of AI. A qualitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, and exploratory-descriptive study was conducted. Twenty key informants from various Ecuadorian public institutions were selected using purposive sampling. The results revealed uneven and evolving institutional readiness. While institutions possess basic digital infrastructure, receptive staff, and initial experience with AI tools, they exhibit limitations in interoperability, specialized training, planning, and systematization of AI adoption. The main gaps were concentrated in governance, the absence of specific protocols, data protection, transparency, human oversight, and the definition of responsibilities. The study concludes that the responsible adoption of AI requires the joint strengthening of technological, human, organizational, and regulatory capacities. The main challenge lies in bridging the gap between emerging technologies and the institutional maturity needed to integrate AI securely, traceably, and in a way that strengthens Ecuadorian public administration.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: CarD-T is an automated pipeline that combines transformer-based machine learning with probabilistic analysis to identify potential carcinogens from biomedical literature. The framework processes accumulating scientific publications, applies a trained Named Entity Recognition (NER) model to extract potential carcinogenic entities, and Probabilistic Carcinogen Denomination (or PCarD) to analyze temporal trends in evidence shifts. This approach enables classification of candidates through Bayesian temporal analysis, overcoming limitations of traditional manual literature review methods.

Aim. To develop a conceptual career management model for academic staff that integrates adaptation, professional development, and leadership into a single management cycle. Objectives. To systematize existing approaches to career management for academic staff and identify their limitations; to develop a five-level model that ensures the transition from adaptation to leadership based on the integration of formal, informal, and self-regulated forms of learning; to delineate the levels of transformation of the subjective position of the teacher and the administration in the process of career development. Methods. The research is based on the systems theory of career development, the model of three forms of workplace learning (formal, informal, and self-regulated), and the level model Architecture – Infrastructure – Access – Practice. The analysis of sources was conducted using a problem-oriented review method. To validate the model, an expert assessment protocol was developed, including a questionnaire for a semi-structured interview and a self-assessment checklist of organizational readiness. Results. A five-level career management model for academic staff is substantiated, providing for preboarding, socialization and self-regulation, collective support practices, institutional design, and reflective control. Each level relies on empirically confirmed mechanisms and performs a function absent in existing approaches. The key result of the model is a change in the logic of management: the administration does not create a career for the teacher but creates conditions and tools that allow the teacher to independently construct a trajectory. The model fills the gaps reflected in scholarly sources, takes into account all stages of the career and the macro context, and integrates institutional conditions, human resource practices, support networks, and behavioral patterns into a single system. Conclusions. A career management system aimed at forming a leader must transform from directive management to environmental management, from control to facilitation. At the input of the system, management means ensuring transparency and safety at the stage preceding the first working day. Within the organization, management is transformed into cultivating an environment in which assistance and learning become everyday practices of employees. In the strategic perspective, management is seen as providing a set of tools and trajectories from which the teacher independently determines their path. The practical significance of the model is ensured by the developed expert assessment protocol, which allows it to be adapted to the conditions of a specific university. The scientific significance lies in the integration of disparate research directions within a single conceptual framework. Prospects for further research are associated with the empirical verification of the model, the development of tools for diagnosing self-regulated learning, and the study of the conditions for the sustainability of collective leadership behaviors.

The increasing competition in the employment market has created significant challenges for students and job seekers in preparing effective resumes, identifying relevant skills, and performing effectively in interviews. Existing career-support systems commonly address individual tasks such as resume screening, job recommendation, or interview preparation, while providing limited integration and personalization. This paper proposes CareerPilot AI, an intelligent career assistance system that integrates resume analysis, Applicant Tracking System evaluation, job-description matching, skill-gap identification, AI-based mock interviews, response evaluation, and personalized learning-roadmap generation. The proposed system uses Natural Language Processing, Large Language Models, semantic matching, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation to process user information and generate context-aware recommendations. A web-based architecture using Streamlit and FastAPI or Flask is proposed, with PDF parsing libraries for resume extraction and vector databases for retrieval-based services. The evaluation framework measures resume parsing accuracy, resume-job matching performance, skill-gap identification, interview-response evaluation, response time, and usability. The system is designed to provide an integrated digital career mentor that connects a candidate's current profile with target job requirements and subsequent preparation activities. Actual experimental results will be obtained after implementation and testing.

Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination from spatio-temporal check-in data, and serves as the foundation for many location-based services. Recent advances incorporate large language models (LLMs) into this task by textualizing user trajectories to exploit their semantic reasoning ability. However, directly generating POI identifiers with such models is unreliable: POIs are sparse, localized, and long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics, which creates a semantic-to-entity gap between high-level mobility intent and concrete POI prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose ANCHOR, a category-anchored framework for semantic-to-entity grounding in next POI recommendation. Specifically, ANCHOR first estimates category-level mobility intent in a compact and stable semantic space, rather than predicting concrete POI entities directly. The inferred intent is then grounded into a candidate set by integrating three complementary sources of mobility evidence: category anchors, historical visit memory, and user preferences. Finally, a history-aware reranker selects the target POI by matching each candidate with the user's historical mobility patterns and current context. Experiments on three real-world check-in datasets show that ANCHOR consistently outperforms representative traditional, structure-enhanced, and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of semantic-to-entity grounding and show favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality, and inference efficiency.

Subject choice of undergraduate students has shifted from the traditional ones to the market-oriented ones such as computer and allied health sciences. This trend is more felt in the recent years in many public sectors universities in Pakistan which are forced to close certain disciplines while opening market oriented courses and degrees to attract students. This study aimed to find out the factors responsible for this trend. A qualitative research design was used in which data was collected from 20 participants (10 students and 10 faculty members) purposively selected from different disciplines at University of Peshawar, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Thematic analysis was used as data analysis techniques, leading to the emergence of five themes: intrinsic motivation and aptitude; evolving subjects and marketability; social desirability, influence of family, peer, social media, and subject prestige; the purported neoliberalism; and the increasing marketability and importance of disciplines such as computer sciences and allied health sciences. These results show that students' choices of subjects are the result of various determinants including personal, social, economic, structural and technological. Students are more likely to study technology and health-related areas due to the improved marketability and employment opportunities, while the traditional disciplines of social sciences and humanities are seen as limiting their chances of employment and reducing their social standing.

This exploratory study analyzes the pedagogical mediation conditions under which ChatGPT's intervention in mathematical modeling amplifies coordination among semiotic registers and favors functional thinking. Twelve second-year secondary school students participated in four teams that modeled the rectilinear motion of a person captured on video and constructed piecewise linear functions. From the articulation between the theory of semiotic representations and Realistic Mathematics Education, the study documented how the teams coordinated the four registers when interacting with ChatGPT. The analysis identifies four conditions that made that mediation productive: the selection of a contextualized situation, the iterative refinement of the prompt, the open stance of the teacher, and the availability of multiple representations as an object of contrast. Given its limited scope, the results offer a first approach to how generative artificial intelligence redistributes cognitive work toward conceptual analysis, and require replication in other groups.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, its implications for teacher candidates’ cognitive processes warrant closer attention. This mixed-methods study examined the use of ChatGPT during lesson planning in the teaching practicum, focusing on perceived cognitive load, patterns of material use, and teacher candidates’ experiences. Twenty-four fourth-year teacher candidates participated in a six-week implementation in which they used ChatGPT to prepare lesson plans and instructional activities. Quantitative data were collected using a cognitive load rating scale, and qualitative data were obtained from weekly reflective narratives. Perceived cognitive load decreased significantly following the six-week implementation. Participants were also more likely to use ChatGPT-generated activities directly than activities obtained from Internet sources. Qualitative findings indicated that ChatGPT supported idea generation, access to instructional content, lesson-plan development, and time efficiency, while participants also reported limitations such as insufficient or repetitive content, misalignment with learning objectives, and system-related problems. Overall, ChatGPT may support lesson planning when its outputs are critically evaluated and adapted to pedagogical needs.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence in higher education is transforming how academic work is produced and legitimized, raising questions about the governance of academic integrity. Current discussions tend to frame integrity as student misconduct, giving less attention to shifts in institutional expectations and educational practices associated with AI-assisted learning. This study examines how international AI policy discourse constructs academic integrity in higher education and allocates responsibility for ethical AI use among institutional actors. Drawing on Bourdieu's theory of practice and Laclau's notion of floating signifiers, it proposes the changing cheating habitus as an analytical concept for examining how dispositions towards authorship and legitimate academic participation might change with the conditions of academic work. The study applies Critical Discourse Analysis to four UNESCO and OECD publications issued between 2023 and 2026, comprising institutional guidance, policy outlooks and a UNESCO-commissioned anthology. Fairclough's three-dimensional framework is used to examine how academic integrity is constructed across the textual, discursive and social dimensions of policy discourse. The findings suggest that responsibility, transparency, trust, authenticity and responsible use act as floating signifiers. They provide normative coherence but remain operationally underdefined across institutional contexts. This ambiguity is embedded in contemporary AI governance discourse. Its effects arise through the relationship between policy language, institutional interpretation and established academic conventions. Institutions promote AI integration through narratives of innovation while continuing to regulate academic legitimacy through assumptions of independent authorship and visible intellectual labour. This creates a structural mismatch in which students are encouraged to engage in AI-supported academic work while remaining accountable to integrity frameworks that have not evolved accordingly. The analysis also suggests that enforcement mechanisms may operate as academic capital filters if differences in academic capital affect the visibility of AI-assisted work. The study defines cheating and being cheated as concurrent structural outcomes arising from governance frameworks that encourage AI use while retaining accountability mechanisms developed before generative AI. It presents academic integrity as structurally mediated and negotiated through discourse. The analysis informs educational leadership and AI governance, especially in rapidly changing contexts such as the United Arab Emirates and the wider Gulf region.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been prominent in our daily lives by means of mobile applications and web search engines. AI-based Automated Essay Scoring (AES) system is playing an increasingly important role in higher education field. This study investigated the relationship between Chinese private university EFL students’ perceived interactivity of iWrite AES system and perceived performance, confirmation, individual innovativeness of AES system, as well as their reflective thinking, and how the variables influence students’ criticism of AES system. Based on a sample of 442 students, the study used Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) for data analysis. The findings indicated that students’ perceived interactivity of AES system is positively related to perceived performance and confirmation. Students’ perceived performance of AES system has a significant influence on students’ confirmation. Furthermore, students’ confirmation of AES system positively affects individual innovativeness, reflective thinking and criticism of AES. And students’ individual innovativeness also positively influences students’ reflective thinking of AES. However, students’ individual innovativeness and reflective thinking of AES system doesn’t have a positive relationship with students’ criticism. This study not only reveals Chinese private university EFL students’ attitudes and experiences towards technological tools but also provide valuable support for enhancing teaching effectiveness and improving teaching methods.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems provide critical computation services in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet (MII), and their resilience depends on timely diagnosis of hazards across the data, AI pipeline, and cyber-physical layers. During operation, new hazard types keep emerging with only a few samples each, hazards co-occur, and the diagnosis model runs on memory-constrained computation nodes. Replay-based class-incremental learning (CIL) can learn new hazard classes while revisiting a small memory of past samples, but existing methods assume single-label, balanced streams, store high-dimensional raw samples, and select them independently of the classifier. We propose Class-aware Latent Attention Replay (CLAR), which combines a dual buffer that stores mostly compact latent representations with a few raw samples, an Attention Leverage Score (ALS) that upper-bounds the classifier logit and guides class-balanced reservoir sampling, and an exponential-moving-average teacher that slows latent-space drift. For an idealized buffer model, we prove that the buffer is class-balanced and follows an ALS-weighted class distribution, and that below a critical per-class capacity, ALS-guided replay has a lower replay-gradient error than class-balanced uniform replay. In the case study, On hazard diagnosis data from an MII testbed, CLAR achieves the highest mean average weighted F1 score among the evaluated replay methods with the same buffer size

BACKGROUND: Stroke-related complications and frequent feeding interruptions often compromise nutritional intake, making enteral nutrition (EN) a cornerstone therapy to improve nutritional status and support recovery. Nevertheless, constipation is highly prevalent and clinically consequential among stroke patients receiving EN, particularly in critically ill populations, where enteral nutrition-associated constipation can impede rehabilitation, increase complications and prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay. AIM: This study aimed to explore potentially important determinants of enteral nutrition-associated constipation (ENAC) in patients with stroke using artificial intelligence approaches, characterise relevant clinical subgroups, compare internally validated machine-learning models and examine how the temporal availability of candidate predictors may influence model performance. STUDY DESIGN: Clinical data from patients admitted to a neurological intensive care unit between December 2019 and December 2023 were retrospectively analysed. K-means clustering was used to identify clinical subgroups. Six algorithms-logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting tree, XGBoost, LightGBM and Table PFN-3-were compared under temporally restricted and expanded retrospective feature frameworks using five repeats of nested five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using ROC-AUC, average precision, Brier score, calibration and decision-curve analysis. Treatment outcomes were summarised descriptively. RESULTS: Among 362 patients, 233 (64.4%) had documented constipation. Table PFN-3 achieved the highest discrimination in both frameworks. The temporally restricted model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.629 (95% CI 0.567-0.689), whereas the expanded retrospective model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.771 (95% CI 0.715-0.820), average precision of 0.857, Brier score of 0.177 and calibration slope of 0.965. The ROC-AUC increased by 0.142 (95% CI 0.090-0.201) after full-hospitalisation information was included. K-means clustering retained three subgroups (K = 3; silhouette coefficient = 0.108), with constipation frequencies of 67.35%, 56.98% and 88.89% in Clusters 0, 1 and 2, respectively. Among evaluable patients, observed relief was 80.3% with glycerin enema, 60.0% with lactulose, 72.7% with combination treatment and 65.7% with neither treatment; these treatment comparisons were descriptive. CONCLUSIONS: Table PFN-3 achieved the strongest internally validated performance, with the expanded retrospective framework combining good discrimination, strong precision-recall performance and close calibration. The 0.142 increase in ROC-AUC after completed hospital-course variables were incorporated quantifies the substantial discriminative information that emerges as hospitalisation evolves. Together with the distinct clinical phenotypes and descriptive treatment findings, these results establish a clinically relevant framework for trajectory-aware bowel monitoring and provide a clear rationale for developing dynamic, time-updated prediction models. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: By integrating machine-learning benchmarking, clinical phenotyping and observed treatment outcomes, this study identifies prolonged, treatment-intensive hospital trajectories as a particularly high-burden constipation phenotype and demonstrates that classification performance changes materially as hospital-course information accumulates. These findings support structured reassessment of bowel risk during neurological intensive care rather than reliance on a single static evaluation and provide a practical rationale for future dynamic monitoring tools.

Generative AI could be the most powerful equaliser in the history of education, putting a patient, personalised tutor within reach of every child. It could equally widen the gap between advantaged and disadvant‐ aged learners, because new technologies usually reach those with re‐ sources first and those without last, if at all. This article draws on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside data on connectivity, refugee education, aid and AI develop‐ ment policy. It argues that the outcome will not be decided by the techno‐ logy but by deliberate choices, and that leaving AI to markets and chance will produce the worse outcome. It identifies four layers of the AI divide: access, skilled guidance, language and culture, and recognition of what learners achieve. It then examines the weakest link in global education, learners in crisis and displacement, where 5.8 million refugee children were out of school in 2025 and international aid fell by nearly a quarter in a single year. It reviews approaches that work where power, connectivity and funding cannot be assumed, including offline platforms, AI delivered through basic phones, support for community teachers and portable, re‐ cognised certificates, along with their risks. It proposes a six-question equity test for any AI decision in education.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Bangladesh's impending transition from least-developed-country status and the initialling of a Framework Agreement on Comprehensive Partnership and Cooperation with the European Union open a structured opportunity to redesign the bilateral economic relationship. This paper develops the concept of a humane trading architecture in which enterprise competitiveness and innovation capacity function as the principal transmission mechanisms between preferential market access and structural transformation. It integrates multidimensional market-measurement tools (the Economic Vulnerability Index and the Environmental Performance Index), mild-form transaction authentication and data validation for small and medium enterprise trade finance, sovereign computational capacity (including a Bangla large language model embedded in digital public infrastructure), and post-quantum readiness for trade finance. Drawing on comparative lessons from the EU–Vietnam Free Trade Agreement and EU–India negotiations, the paper specifies five negotiating redlines, co-creation pathways in food, fuel and finance, and a three-phase roadmap calibrated to the current United Nations graduation schedule and the pending request for a preparatory extension. The resulting framework preserves strategic autonomy while extending economic franchise to domestic firms and workers. Personal academic views only.
topics: Global trade, sustainability, and social impact

documents.abstract: The introduction of collaborative robots (cobots) into the workplace has presented both opportunities and challenges for those seeking to utilize their functionality. Prior research has shown that despite the capabilities afforded by cobots, there is a disconnect between those capabilities and the applications in which they are currently deployed, partially due to a lack of effective cobot-focused instruction in the field. Experts who work successfully within this collaborative domain could offer insight into the considerations and processes they use to more effectively capture this cobot capability. Using an analysis of expert insights in the collaborative interaction design space, we developed a set of Expert Frames based on these insights and integrated these Expert Frames into a new training and programming system and evaluated how automated expert feedback supports novice troubleshooting and user perception. We evaluated our system with novice and expert users to understand their experience and expectations for robot programming.

Individual differences in cognitive abilities may influence how people form and adjust trust in automated systems, yet the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. This study investigated how three foundational cognitive abilities - working memory (WM), attention control (AC), and fluid intelligence (Gf) - shape trust dynamics, particularly focusing on trust decline and recovery after automation failures. Participants (N = 111) completed cognitive tests measuring WM, AC, and Gf before performing a dual-task paradigm where they monitored an automated memory aid exhibiting varying reliability levels (100%-65%-100%) while completing an arithmetic task. Results revealed that WM and Gf positively predicted trust recovery after automation failures, while AC influenced long-term trust calibration, with high-AC individuals showing more nuanced trust adjustments reflecting system reliability history. Trust decline was uniform across ability levels, suggesting that trust loss may occur rapidly after salient failures. The relationship between abilities and trust may have been partially mediated by automation schemas, with WM negatively correlating with all-or-none thinking about automation. These findings suggest different cognitive abilities play distinct roles in trust dynamics: WM supports monitoring automation performance, Gf enables effective schema updating, and AC facilitates appropriate deployment of these resources for trust calibration. This work advances our understanding of trust mechanisms and has implications for designing automation interfaces that accommodate individual cognitive differences.

This study explores the dimensions and influencing factors of Chinese students’ cognitive engagement in a blended learning environment that integrates offline classroom instruction with online written evaluation (including AI-driven automated written evaluation and human-based evaluation). By analyzing data from questionnaires, semi-structured interviews, writing drafts, and feedback, the findings reveal that: (1) students’ cognitive engagement in blended learning is indicated by their attention, cognitive and metacognitive operations, and self-regulation; (2) These dimensions are influenced by a combination of individual and contextual factors, including learner autonomy, study habits, motivation, exams, task difficulty, and instruction mode. This study has significant theoretical and practical implications for enhancing student engagement in blended learning and for the deeper integration of AI into second language (L2) writing instruction.

The paper substantiates the factors that give rise to crisis situations and conflicts during the management of energy-active facilities – situations that frequently escalate into emergencies requiring rapid response and effective decision-making. In such contexts, it is crucial to examine the psychological and intellectual resilience of operators, as this resilience underpins the capacity of systems and agents to function within the scope of defined objectives and authorities. Such resilience serves as a key factor in maintaining functional efficiency when countering various types of threats and attacks. A significant aspect of functional resilience involves analysing the logic behind decision-making aimed at achieving system-oriented outcomes. These decisions are grounded in principles of coherence, multi-level analysis, and risk assessment. Identifying the structure of this management logic and the associated decision-making procedures enables the development of efficient algorithms for addressing crisis situations – algorithms applicable across diverse fields, ranging from security management to socio-economic systems. The challenge of making efficient decisions – whether by an intelligent agent (a team player), an operational team, or a managerial/administrative structure – is determined by a complex interplay of psycho-neurophysiological and intellectual factors, operating at both the individual and team levels. They are participants in a game structure that shapes the strategy of permissible actions. To address this problem, the paper develops a cognitive-logical concept for the operational resilience of cyber-physical infrastructure, which integrates a “human-agent” into a unified situational control loop. Based on the category algebra, a category-theoretic information model is constructed for the decomposition of a hierarchical production structure, accounting for 16 threat-resilient personnel levels (P1–P16). By integrating H. Gardner’s theory of multiple intelligences and R. Sternberg’s triarchic theory, a cognitive map for operator decision-making during laser-based environmental monitoring is formalized. A mathematical framework for the quantitative assessment of personnel actions is developed, incorporating cognitive coefficients (KF), confidence levels (K(B)), and error risk factors (Ri). Practical testing of the system at the Burshtyn Power Station (Ukraine) and glass-manufacturing companies has demonstrated its efficiency under extreme operating conditions (1200°C–1500°C). Implementation of this method has reduced the reaction time of operational and dispatch personnel during pre-emergency and emergency conditions (Alarm/Avaria) and minimized the overall risk of error decisions stemming from the human factor.

PURPOSE: This study aimed to explore the convergent validity of two widely used virtual reality (VR) haptic dental simulators, Simodont and Virteasy, by comparing dental students' performance on comparable abstract psychomotor tasks. Secondary objectives were to examine short-term learning effects, simulator order, and the potential influence of additional clinical exposure. METHODS: A two-period crossover study was conducted with 74 fourth-year dental students corresponding to 222 paired exercise datasets. Each participant completed three progressively complex tasks (direct line, indirect line, indirect cross) on both simulators, 6 months apart. Primary outcome measures were the percentage of target removed on Simodont and the percentage of progression achieved on Virteasy. Secondary outcomes included simulator-specific scores, drill time, and total task time. Paired t-tests and within-subject comparisons were used for analysis. RESULTS: Differences were observed between simulators for target-related metrics and drill time outcomes. Virteasy generated higher target progression values, whereas longer drill times were recorded on this platform. Given the substantial differences in scoring logic, ergonomics, and workflow implementation between systems, these metrics should not be interpreted as indicators of simulator efficiency or learner superiority. No significant period effect was observed (+0.6%, p = 0.36). Both simulators demonstrated short-term learning effects, with the greatest improvement between the first and second attempts. Simulator order had no significant influence on performance. Precision on Virteasy did not correlate with Simodont composite scores. CONCLUSIONS: Both simulators supported effective psychomotor task execution but produced non-equivalent performance outcomes due to differences in feedback, ergonomics, and scoring logic. These findings support the view that Simodont and Virteasy assess partially overlapping constructs rather than interchangeable competencies. Future research should focus on mapping simulator-specific metrics to defined competency frameworks rather than harmonizing scores across platforms.

Self-evolving agent skills enable AI agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. However, since such skills are typically represented as textual documents and executed through LLM reasoning, even previously learned procedures must be repeatedly interpreted and regenerated, introducing avoidable uncertainty into every execution. In contrast, program execution is deterministic and independently verifiable. Intuitively, transforming well-specified operations into executable programs can reduce reliance on LLM reasoning and, consequently, reduce execution uncertainty. Motivated by this intuition, we introduce SKillCompiler, a self-evolving skill framework that integrates programmatic compilation into the skill evolution process. Specifically, SkillCompiler adopts an executability-aware skill compilation strategy that decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability, and constructs hybrid skill skeletons that retain LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations while compiling well-specified ones into validated programs. To avoid redundant program synthesis and enable executable knowledge to accumulate across evolving skills, we further design a program asset reuse mechanism that organizes validated programs as reusable assets, retrieves existing implementations whenever applicable, and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and six model families demonstrate that SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33\% improvement in task performance.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from promise to routine practice in clinical and translational research, and large language models (LLMs) are now used to scope analyses, draft and debug code, and accelerate the quantitative work that supports clinical and translational decisions. This adoption is outpacing the operational safeguards that keep such work reproducible and auditable, and the central risk is not only erroneous code but the quieter erosion of the analytical discipline on which trustworthy bench‐to‐bedside decisions depend. In this position paper, we argue that AI can be integrated into regulated quantitative workflows without sacrificing reproducibility, provided it operates inside a compliance‐by‐design architecture built on two principles: analytical intent must be formally encoded and locked before execution, and the analysis itself must run outside the LLM as specification‐verified code in a validated environment. We describe three failure modes that ordinary quality control does not detect, namely context drift, the displacement effect, and implementation drift, and we link each to documented model behavior. For open‐ended investigation, these principles are operationalized as a four‐step execution firewall; for recurring development studies such as assay validations and animal safety studies, they are operationalized through a governed library of documented, validated agents, supported by fit‐for‐purpose validation, a clear separation of human and machine roles, and post‐deployment monitoring. Both approaches can be implemented with components available today. Used this way, AI enhances rather than replaces quantitative expertise, which now resides less in the code a model produces than in the constraints a scientist defines before it runs.
